region: West Central Africa (Gabon, Cameroon, Republic of the Congo)
description: Zebrawood is a heavy African hardwood with bold dark stripes on a pale gold background, used mostly as veneer and for accent pieces, boxes, handles and turned work.

hazards.summary: A worker developed asthma from zebrawood dust; a skin test, a bronchial challenge and a blood allergy test all confirmed sensitivity, while unexposed people did not react. The report identified the wood to the genus Microberlinia.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: Applies to wood dust generally; this species has no separate ACGIH value.

related_species_note: Zebrawood in trade comes from Microberlinia brazzavillensis and the closely related M. bisulcata; the asthma report did not name the species.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed zebrawood (Microberlinia brazzavillensis) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Heartwood a light golden-straw to pale tan background with sharply contrasting narrow dark brown to near-black stripes running along the board. Quartersawn face showing straight, parallel zebra-like striping, coarse texture with visible open pores and interlocked grain giving slight shimmer. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of zebrawood with pale gold wood and bold dark brown parallel stripes.
notes_internal: Bush-1978 identifies only genus Microberlinia, so species-level attribution to M. brazzavillensis is by trade convention; M. bisulcata also sold as zebrawood. Zebrawood is not listed in HSE-WIS30 (rev1 2012). Common names zebrano and the M. bisulcata note are from general knowledge, not a cited source; verify against BS EN 13556 or an FPL sheet.
